evals.prompt: I'm the platform lead at Ledgerline. We expose a gRPC API (12 services, protobuf) to about 40 fintech partners. Errors today come back as a bare UNKNOWN status with a prose string. I want to build a proper error-code catalog like Stripe's: a flat list of codes, each mapped to an HTTP status code, published on our docs site. Can you design the taxonomy? We're a Google Cloud shop and the team lives in gRPC daily. No REST gateway, and no plans for one.
evals.expected_output: A taxonomy design that rejects the requested HTTP-status-pinned flat catalog and delivers a domain/reason (AIP-193 ErrorInfo) taxonomy, with the stability contract and a published catalog of every (domain, reason) pair.
expectations: Recommends the domain/reason taxonomy (Google AIP-193 ErrorInfo style) instead of the flat HTTP-status-pinned catalog the user asked for
States that HTTP-status-pinned catalog shapes (flat catalog and code/subcode) are removed from the menu entirely on a gRPC-only surface, not merely ranked last or discouraged
Justifies the removal by the fact that those shapes define each code's identity by pinning it to one HTTP status, which a gRPC-only surface does not have
Rejects any 'we'll map codes to HTTP statuses later' compromise, or names the re-promotion condition explicitly as a REST surface joining the API family
Defines the stable machine-readable identity as the (domain, reason) pair
Includes a metadata map on the error for dynamic context values
Notes that the team's existing gRPC/Google Cloud fluency lowers the usual adoption effort of domain/reason substantially
References google.rpc.Status carrying ErrorInfo in its details, or cites AIP-193 by name
States the stability contract: a (domain, reason) pair stays consistent over time and its metadata keys can only be added, never removed or repurposed
States that the human-readable message text is not contractually stable and client code must never parse or match on it
Requires every reason a client can ever see to be enumerable ahead of time in one published catalog, and treats a reason invented ad hoc at a call site without a catalog entry as a design defect
The delivered catalog design does not assign an HTTP status code to each error identity

evals.prompt: Our REST API at Parcelbyte (shipping-label SaaS, roughly 900 external integrators) has three different error shapes: /v1/labels returns {"success": false, "error": "..."} with HTTP 200, /v1/rates returns {"message", "status"} with proper 4xx codes, and the newer endpoints return {"errors": [...]}. A new backend lead wants to design one clean custom JSON error envelope from scratch, something like {ok, errorCode, errorText}. Before we build it, what should the envelope be? One more thing: today we return 400 when the address payload is well-formed JSON but fails our business validation rules.
evals.expected_output: An envelope design that adopts RFC 9457 problem details with extension members instead of the proposed custom envelope, fixes the status codes first (including the 200-with-error endpoint and the 400-vs-422 case), and treats the retrofit as a contract-preserving migration.
expectations: Recommends RFC 9457 problem details and rejects building the proposed custom {ok, errorCode, errorText} envelope
Names RFC 9457 as the standard to design against, not RFC 7807 alone
Specifies the media type application/problem+json
Uses the standard fields type, title, status, detail, and instance

Attaches the machine-readable taxonomy through extension members on the problem-details body (such as code, errors, retryable, documentation_url, request_id) rather than through a parallel non-standard envelope
States that the correct HTTP status must be picked first because the body explains the status and never replaces it, with intermediaries (proxies, caches, monitors) reading only the status
Flags the /v1/labels 200-with-success:false shape as a wrong-status defect to eliminate
Recommends 422 for the well-formed-but-semantically-invalid address case, distinguishing it explicitly from 400 for malformed requests
Requires one identical envelope on every endpoint and every status
Treats envelope consistency as binary: a single deviating endpoint fails the audit
Treats already-shipped codes, fields, and message strings as potentially depended-on by clients (Hyrum's Law) and maps old identities to new ones instead of silently dropping them
Structures the audit of the current surface as a table with one row per endpoint covering items such as status returned, envelope shape, code presence, retry signal, and documentation
Asks, or explicitly accounts for, which codes and fields existing integrators already branch on before changing them

evals.prompt: We're localizing the Craftpoint API (B2B inventory management) for French and German integrators. Product wants every part of the error response translated based on the customer's locale, including the short error identifiers, so INVALID_SKU would come back as REFERENCE_INVALIDE for French accounts. Separately, our current messages are strings like MIN_QTY_RULE_VIOLATED with nothing else attached. Can you spec the localized error design and rewrite an example? A failing request to work from: quantity=0 sent to POST /v1/stock-moves, where the minimum is 1.
evals.expected_output: A localization spec that refuses to translate error codes, localizes only the prose via Accept-Language/Content-Language, and rewrites the message to name field, received value, and constraint with structured detail.
expectations: Refuses to translate the error code: code values like INVALID_SKU stay untranslated for every locale
Justifies the refusal by the code being the field client code logs, branches, and matches on
Localizes only the human-readable message/detail text, negotiated via the Accept-Language request header
Echoes the chosen language back in a Content-Language response header
Mentions the alternative split of keeping the message stable and developer-facing while carrying translated end-user text in a separate localized-message field
The rewritten error names the field, the value received, and the constraint violated in the same error object (quantity, received 0, minimum 1)
Includes structured machine-readable detail such as the provided value and the constraint (e.g. value_provided 0, min 1), not prose alone
Uses corrective, non-blaming phrasing in the rewritten message rather than accusatory phrasing like 'you entered an invalid quantity'
Evaluates messages against three independent properties - human-readable, actionable, consistent in format across the API - checked separately
Identifies the MIN_QTY_RULE_VIOLATED-style bare rule name as the failure pattern: a rule named with no field, no expected value, and no self-serve path
For errors whose fix takes a paragraph to explain, links a documentation_url to the code's catalog entry instead of cramming the explanation into the message
Keeps structured fields as the machine signal so the prose message is never the only thing a programmatic caller can branch on

evals.prompt: Cleanup task at Meterhaus, an energy-data API that's been live for 5 years with about 2,300 API consumers. Our error codes are a mess: ERR_17, billing_failed, INVALID-METER, all different conventions. For the next release of the error surface I want to rename everything in place to one consistent SCREAMING_SNAKE scheme - for example billing_failed simply becomes BILLING_FAILED - and drop about a dozen codes nobody should be using anymore. We control the docs, so we'll update the docs page the same day. Sketch the migration.
evals.expected_output: A migration plan that refuses the in-place rename and silent deletions, treats shipped codes as contract under Hyrum's Law, evolves by addition only, retires codes only through versioned deprecation, and installs a catalog with declared stability and a gatekeeper.
expectations: Refuses the in-place rename of shipped error codes, treating error codes as API contract whose change is a breaking change
Invokes Hyrum's Law: with enough users, someone depends on every observable behavior, including undocumented codes and message text
Refuses to silently drop the dozen codes, noting that 'nobody should be using them' is not evidence nobody does
States the evolution rule as addition only: new codes and new optional fields may be added freely, but a shipped code is never repurposed, renamed, or deleted
Routes any code retirement through the API's deprecation machinery so a code disappears only on a version boundary, never silently
Requires an explicit mapping from every old code identity to its new identity rather than dropping old identities
Declares stability explicitly in the catalog: the code is stable and safe to branch on, while message/detail text may change without notice
Cites the Google-style stability model where the error identity must stay consistent over time and message text is explicitly non-contractual
Installs a catalog gatekeeper - an owner or review step - protecting the invariant that no code reaches production without a catalog entry
Requests 5-10 real production error responses across different endpoints before designing the migration, since this is a retrofit
Asks which codes, fields, or message strings existing clients already branch on, treating those as contract
Flags codes invented ad hoc at call sites and missing from the published catalog as design defects to resolve in the same pass

evals.prompt: Retries question for the Quotamill API, a REST rate-quote engine. Our 500s spiked last week and three integrators hammered us with instant retries. I want the error responses themselves to tell clients when to retry. Draft the retry signaling for us - and include the exact backoff algorithm (multiplier and jitter formula) in the error body spec so every integrator implements the same one. Statuses we currently return: 400, 401, 404, 409, 429, 500, 503.
evals.expected_output: A retry-signaling design scoped to response fields (declining to spec backoff algorithms), with the status-based retryability split, Retry-After on 429 and 503, a retryable boolean in the body, and an explicit retry object on 500.
expectations: Declines to embed the backoff algorithm (multiplier, jitter formula) in the error body spec, scoping this design to signal fields rather than client retry mechanics
States the retryable baseline by status: 429 and 503 retryable (with 408, 502, 504 in the same class), and 500 only sometimes
Marks 400, 401, and 404 as non-retryable
Marks 409 as non-retryable, on the reasoning that repeating the unchanged request fails identically
Requires the Retry-After header on both 429 and 503 as the minimum signal
Justifies Retry-After as a real HTTP header that generic clients and proxies parse without understanding the body format
Includes a retryable true/false boolean in the response body even when the Retry-After header is present

Justifies the body-level boolean: it is the one field a generic error handler branches on without a status-code lookup table, and not every client library surfaces headers as easily as the parsed body
Treats 500 as genuinely ambiguous (transient blip vs real bug) and emits an explicit retry object on 500 rather than letting the caller guess
Names a bare 500 with no retry signal as the design gap to close
Offers a richer body retry object (retryable, retry_after, optional guidance fields) for cases where the header under-specifies the caller's options
Splits severity by who acts: 4xx means the caller should stop and change the request, 5xx means retry later or the provider must fix a bug

evals.prompt: I run developer support at Fieldnest, an agritech API platform. Last month we logged 412 support tickets and 61% were integrators pasting a screenshot of an error and asking what it means - we can almost never trace the original request. On the docs side, every endpoint just links to one shared 'Error object' schema page. Leadership wants a hard target and proposed committing to 'error-related tickets under 10% of volume within a quarter'. How do I fix the error documentation, and how should we measure success?
evals.expected_output: A documentation design with per-endpoint per-code named OpenAPI examples, a single anchored catalog page, request-ID echo in header and body, spec-generated docs, and a measurement frame that rejects the invented 10% threshold in favor of binary gates plus an own-baseline trend.
expectations: Enumerates each status an endpoint can return in its OpenAPI responses block
Requires a named example per distinct error code under each status, rejecting the single generic 'Error object' schema reference
Publishes the error catalog as a single public page with a stable anchor per code
Points documentation_url in error responses at those per-code anchors
Specifies per-code catalog content covering the HTTP status it rides on, what causes it, whether it is retryable, whether its message is safe to show end users, and the fix path
Requires a code to be documented before it ships, never after a support ticket forces it
Returns a request-ID header (such as X-Request-ID) on every response
Echoes the same ID in the error body's request_id field so it survives being copy-pasted into a ticket without the header
Identifies the request-ID echo as the highest-leverage change for converting vague error tickets into traceable ones
Recommends regenerating the published catalog and per-endpoint examples from the spec so documentation and responses cannot drift apart
Rejects committing to the proposed 10%-within-a-quarter target because no industry threshold exists, setting the baseline from the platform's own first month instead
Treats the support-ticket signal as a trend to watch, never as a pass/fail gate
Names the two actual gates: envelope consistency at 100% of endpoints and statuses (binary), and catalog coverage with zero observable codes missing from the catalog or endpoint examples
Tracks the share of error-related tickets that arrive carrying a request ID as a metric

evals.prompt: Designing validation errors for Bindery, a B2B contract-management API. Two cases I'm stuck on. First, POST /v1/agreements validates 30+ fields and our mobile team complains they get one error at a time and must resubmit repeatedly to discover all the problems. Second, we enforce that renewal_date must be at least 30 days after signature_date - my plan is to attach that error to the renewal_date field like any other field error. Also relevant: POST /v1/agreements:bulkImport accepts up to 500 agreements, and when say 20 fail I was going to return 200 with a results array where failed items carry {ok: false, reason: "..."} strings.
evals.expected_output: A validation-error design returning all field failures in one structured errors array, a dedicated cross-field shape for the date rule instead of pinning it to one field, and bulk per-item failures that reuse the standard error shape rather than ad hoc reason strings.
expectations: Returns every failing field in one response through an errors array with multiple entries, instead of one error per resubmission
Gives each field error structured members: the field name, a specific code, a message, the value provided, and the violated constraints
Frames the payoff as one API error mapping to multiple form-field indicators in a single round trip
Rejects attaching the date rule to renewal_date alone: a cross-field constraint is never forced into the single-field shape
Shapes the cross-field error with a fields array naming both fields and a values_provided map carrying both submitted values
Requires the bulk endpoint's per-item failures to reuse the same standard error shape, rejecting the ad hoc {ok: false, reason} string objects
States that a 200 response mixing success and per-item failures is acceptable only for bulk or long-running operations and rejected everywhere else
Uses a specific per-reason code on each field error (such as OUT_OF_RANGE or INVALID_FORMAT) beneath the top-level validation code
Rides the whole validation payload on the API's one standard error envelope with a top-level code pinned to one status
Each message names the field, the value received, and the constraint violated
Keeps structured fields as the signal machine callers branch on, so a prose reason string is never the only information carried
Requires every validation code and sub-reason to appear in the published error catalog, enumerable before a client ever hits it
